title: The next leadership crisis is the 50-Year-Old never taught to lead in a changing world
author: Ghassan Karian
summary: Ghassan Karian challenges the reassuring story that AI will take over routine work while humans keep empathy, judgment and creativity, by asking how many current leaders are actually good at those things. Drawing on the WEF Future of Jobs Report, DDI's Global Leadership Forecast, Gartner and the OECD, he shows a wide gap between what leadership now demands and what organisations are developing. Leaders name strategy and change as their biggest skill gaps, yet only 22 percent of HR teams prioritise them. He argues experienced leaders are hardest to develop because a long record of success makes a command-and-certainty repertoire feel proven, so the change is an identity challenge, and cites Keltner's research on how power erodes empathy. Frontline leaders worry about AI three times more than senior leaders, exposing an empathy gap. Karian concludes that lectures and frameworks fail, and that peer challenge, senior-level coaching and real exposure to uncertainty work better.
points: Leaders identify setting strategy and managing change as their greatest gaps, yet only 22 percent of HR teams prioritise developing them.
Senior leaders are hardest to develop because past success validated a repertoire of command and certainty, making change an identity challenge.
Keltner's power paradox suggests long exposure to power erodes the empathy and curiosity now most in demand.
Senior leaders pushing AI adoption are insulated from the front line, where leaders are three times more concerned about its impact.
Development that works involves structured peer challenge, senior-level coaching and exposure to real uncertainty, while seminars and lectures often have a negative effect.
quotes: The gap between what the role now demands and what the development system is producing is, to use a technical term, enormous.
is not merely a development challenge. It is, for many experienced leaders, an identity challenge.

The leaders with the longest track records have had the longest exposure to the conditions that most corrode those qualities. Their development need is greatest and, yet, their openness to it is frequently lowest.

Senior leaders who are enthusiastic about AI’s potential but insulated from its daily complexity at the front line are making decisions about people who are navigating that complexity without fully understanding what they are navigating through.

What works, the evidence increasingly suggests, is structured peer challenge, sustained coaching by people qualified to work at the senior level, genuine exposure to situations that require the new competencies rather than the old ones, and organisations that reward epistemic humility rather than punishing it.
The next leadership crisis is already visible in the data. The only question is whether organisations are willing to look at it honestly before it arrives in person.
